content: Mutations in the KCNJ11 and ABCC8 genes are associated with neonatal diabetes syndromes. These mutations can result in either transient or permanent neonatal diabetes, depending on the specific nature of the mutation. Infants with these genetic mutations may respond to treatment with oral sulfonylureas instead of requiring insulin therapy. Mutations in the INS gene are linked to permanent neonatal diabetes that necessitates insulin therapy. This mutation disrupts the production of insulin within pancreatic beta cells, leading to the condition. Abnormalities involving the 6q24 region, specifically mutations in the PLAGL1 and HYMAI genes, are associated with transient neonatal diabetes mellitus. This condition is often related to uniparental disomy and may present with symptoms that can recur during adolescence. Mutations in the EIF2AK3 gene cause Wolcott-Rallison Syndrome, a recessive disorder that results in permanent neonatal diabetes. This syndrome is also characterized by additional clinical features, including skeletal abnormalities and liver dysfunction. Mutations in the FOXP3 gene are associated with IPEX Syndrome, an X-linked immune disorder. This condition includes diabetes as a clinical feature, along with other autoimmune and inflammatory symptoms.
